source_metadata.title: A Landscape Analysis of Access, Equity, and Reporting Trends in Digital Health Randomized Controlled Trials
source_metadata.status: Article in Press; unedited accepted manuscript
source_metadata.study_design: LLM-assisted landscape review / information-extraction study of digital health technology-enabled RCT publications

atoms.canonical_statement: The study aimed to measure the global rise of digital health technology-enabled randomized controlled trials and use LLM-assisted mining of published trial outcomes to characterize equity, access, and reporting practices.

The literature search was developed with a Mayo Clinic librarian and used Ovid MEDLINE and related Ovid MEDLINE citation sets through February 8, 2024; the earliest included publication year was 2010 and articles through January 2024 were screened.

The search identified 16,924 records; 9,397 were removed by duplicate and keyword filtering, 7,527 records were screened, 2,075 were excluded by LLM-accelerated screening, and 5,452 reports were included for title/metadata review.
Among the 5,452 eligible reports, the authors extracted 5,298 manuscript abstracts, 4,835 participant eligibility-criteria regions, and 4,304 participant baseline demographic tables.
Eligible publications were programmatically parsed with Python 3.13.3 to isolate study abstract and methods-region content.
Participant baseline demographic tables were extracted from Results sections using optical character recognition with Python-tesseract 5.0.0.
Content-region-specific processed text files were analyzed with standardized prompts using OpenAI GPT-4o through Azure OpenAI Services.

Extracted text was normalized using the ODHT Digital Health Technologies Ontology, a prior digital-health-purpose framework, WHO digital-health user categories, AAMC health specialties, CONSORT 2010 items, and proposed social-determinants-of-health variables.
Sex and gender were aggregated as "Sex or Gender," and race and ethnicity were aggregated as "Race or Ethnicity," because source reporting practices were inconsistent and ambiguous.

For screening evaluation, a gold standard of 587 randomly sampled digital health technology-enabled RCTs was independently screened by two annotators and adjudicated by a third reviewer until 100% consensus was reached.

Full-text extraction performance was evaluated on 90 eligible articles available as 50 PDFs and 40 XML files, with abstract, participant eligibility criteria, and baseline demographic table extraction treated as independent tasks.
The final analytic corpus comprised 5,452 digital health technology-enabled randomized controlled trial outcomes published between 2010 and January 2024.

atoms.canonical_statement: Despite gold-standard curation, the authors note that large language models may perform worse overall than traditional manual extraction.
Heterogeneity in where information appeared and in publisher styling limited machine-assisted parsing and reduced the sample available for some extraction tasks.
Inconsistent and ambiguous reporting of sex versus gender and race versus ethnicity complicated accurate extraction and classification.
Some identity characteristics, including immigration status, were not extracted because they were minimally reported in the source literature.
The authors conclude that global collaboration and consensus on common data elements are needed to improve the equity, accessibility, and consistency of digital health trial reporting.
The authors call for future work to standardize documentation of technology interventions and study-population characteristics in digital health technology-enabled randomized controlled trials.

The work was supported by the U.S. National Library of Medicine (R01LM011934) and the Cancer Prevention Institute of Texas (RR230020); the authors state that the funders had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, or manuscript writing.

Hongfang Liu was an Editorial Board Member of npj Digital Medicine but was not involved in the review or decision on the manuscript; the authors declared no further competing financial or non-financial interests.
The datasets generated and analyzed for the study and all code used in the manuscript are publicly available in the OHNLP/ACCEL GitHub repository.

extraction_limitations: The supplied source is an Article in Press unedited manuscript and explicitly warns that errors may remain before final publication.
Supplementary Notes 1 and 2 are referenced in the manuscript but were not included in the supplied 19-page PDF; no atoms were created from unavailable supplementary content.

This study is a landscape review of RCT publications rather than a patient-level randomized trial. For aggregate quantitative-result atoms, the current LiteratureAtom schema requires an exposures field, so the analyzed publication corpus is represented as an exposure context; this is a schema-mapping compromise rather than a causal exposure claim.
Several user and technology-purpose categories are reported by the authors as non-mutually exclusive; their percentages should not be interpreted as mutually exclusive partitions.
No external sources were used to correct, update, or verify the manuscript; extracted atoms reflect the supplied source only.
